# Two-year roadmap toward graduate-level quantitative research

Prepared 7 October 2026. Planning window: October 2026–September 2028.

Personal starting point: undergraduate in robotics and AI; builds agentic workflows; independently solves roughly 800–1000-rated Codeforces problems in C++; willing to relocate; mathematics preparation not yet established.

This roadmap combines verified employer requirements, university curricula, competition rules, and research sources with my proposed study sequence. Time allocations, proficiency targets, project choices, and application priorities are recommendations, not requirements imposed by those institutions. Competition eligibility and job availability are snapshots; verify the relevant edition and posting when applying.

## 1. Define an achievable destination

The two-year stretch target is **working competence in selected early-PhD subjects and supervised research readiness**, not a completed PhD or equivalence to an experienced quantitative researcher. If calculus, linear algebra, and proof writing are currently weak, a strong undergraduate foundation plus initial graduate courses is the more realistic outcome. Neither outcome implies admission or a job offer.

Actual doctoral programs distinguish coursework from original research. Stanford Statistics tests probability, theoretical statistics, and applied statistics after its first-year program; candidacy also requires a faculty judgment of research potential. CMU's ML doctorate combines advanced coursework with research from the first semester. These are useful benchmarks, not credentials that self-study can confer. [Stanford qualifying examinations](https://statistics.stanford.edu/academic-programs/graduate-programs/phd-program/doctoral-program/doctoral-program-qualifying-exams), [CMU ML PhD curriculum](https://www.ml.cmu.edu/current-students/phd-curriculum.html).

By month 24, aim to demonstrate:

1. Probability and statistical reasoning through unseen written problems and oral explanations.
2. Ability to formulate and solve an optimization problem, then explain its numerical limitations.
3. A reproducible empirical research pipeline with chronological validation and an experiment registry.
4. Two carefully documented replications, one of which becomes a supervised extension.
5. A substantial research manuscript, presentation, and external technical review.
6. One meaningful research assistantship or internship, if available; otherwise an equivalent supervised project with regular feedback.
7. Enough coding and communication ability to interview for appropriate student roles.

Publications, competition medals, and profitable signals are possible outcomes, not prerequisites for finishing this plan. A well-executed negative result can demonstrate research judgment.

## 2. Choose a research direction

| Track | Typical research questions | Preparation to emphasize | Fit for you |
|---|---|---|---|
| Statistical ML and systematic investing | Which features predict returns, volatility, or risk? Does a result survive realistic validation? | Probability, inference, time series, optimization, asset pricing, data engineering | Recommended default |
| Market microstructure, execution, and market making | How do orders affect prices? How should quotes and inventory respond to uncertainty? | Event-level data, point processes, control, C++, execution models | Strong robotics connection; pursue if good data and supervision become available |
| Derivatives pricing | How should an option or structured product be priced and hedged? | Stochastic calculus, PDEs, numerical methods, calibration | Viable alternative; requires a different second-year emphasis |
| Quantitative risk and model validation | Does a model measure exposure reliably? When does it fail? | Statistics, stress testing, derivatives, numerical analysis | Useful adjacent pathway; research content depends on the team |

Your suggested specialization is **sequential statistical learning and uncertainty estimation for financial time series**. State estimation, Bayesian filtering, system identification, and control are natural bridges from robotics. Do not assume markets behave like stationary physical systems: feedback, competition, changing incentives, and noisy measurements must be part of the model.

Choose one principal track by month 12. You cannot credibly master ML research, high-frequency trading, advanced derivatives, and portfolio management simultaneously in two years.

Keep agentic workflow engineering as a supporting strength. Use it to retrieve papers, manage experiments, reproduce results, and generate auditable reports. The intellectual contribution must still be a well-posed question, valid method, and defensible result.

Employer evidence supports this emphasis. Citadel's BS/MS research internship asks for probability and statistics, research experience, and the ability to translate models into code. Two Sigma's campus researcher posting welcomes degree levels from bachelor's through doctorate and asks for an in-depth project using real data. HRT calls its research-oriented student role Algorithm Development. [Citadel BS/MS internship](https://www.citadel.com/careers/details/quantitative-research-analyst-intern-bs-ms-europe/), [Two Sigma campus research role](https://careers.twosigma.com/careers/JobDetail/New-York-New-York-United-States-Quantitative-Researcher-Full-Time-Campus-Hire/13258), [HRT student opportunities](https://www.hudsonrivertrading.com/student-opportunities/).

## 3. First two weeks: diagnose mathematics before accelerating

Your Codeforces level establishes some independent programming ability; it does not establish probability, numerical computing, or research maturity. Do not use it as a substitute for a mathematics assessment.

Use unfamiliar exercises under closed-book conditions, then review mistakes. A lecturer or teaching assistant should inspect at least some of the solutions.

| Area | Diagnostic tasks | Repair if weak |
|---|---|---|
| Calculus | Differentiate a multivariable loss; compute a gradient and Hessian; use Taylor approximation; evaluate basic integrals | Calculus and multivariable calculus before advanced probability/optimization |
| Linear algebra | Solve a least-squares problem; explain rank, eigenvectors, projections, PSD matrices, and SVD | A full introductory linear algebra course |
| Probability | Conditional probability, Bayes' rule, expectation, variance, covariance, and common distributions | A full calculus-based probability course |
| Proofs | Induction, contradiction, quantifiers, an epsilon-delta argument, convergence of a sequence | Introductory proofs followed by real analysis |
| Programming | Parse a file; aggregate by date; simulate random variables; implement and test a regression | Scientific Python and numerical programming |
| Statistics | Distinguish a confidence interval from a predictive interval; explain assumptions of a test | Introductory inference before graduate statistics |

If multiple foundations are weak, reserve months 1–6 for repair and remove an advanced second-year elective. If the diagnostic is strong, advance faster through the first six months and deepen the later graduate material. Do not remove research supervision to preserve an ambitious course list.

## 4. Knowledge map and dependency order

The main chain is:

**Calculus + linear algebra + proofs → probability + introductory inference → regression + optimization → time series + graduate statistics → specialization + independent research.**

### 4.1 Mathematics

**Core, months 1–6:** multivariable calculus; gradients and Hessians; vector spaces; projections; least squares; eigendecomposition and SVD; positive semidefinite matrices; basic numerical conditioning; proof writing; sequences, continuity, and convergence.

**Graduate bridge, months 7–15:** sigma-algebras, measurable random variables, integration, kỳ vọng có điều kiện, các dạng hội tụ, dominated convergence, laws of large numbers, định lý giới hạn trung tâms, bất đẳng thức tập trung, finite Markov chains, and martingale basics.

**Optimization, months 7–18:** convex sets and functions, first/second-order conditions, Lagrange multipliers, KKT conditions, duality, gradient and proximal methods, constrained quadratic programs, tối ưu hóa ngẫu nhiên, and numerical stability.

**Specialization only:** Itô calculus, SDEs, PDEs, stochastic control, point processes, or high-dimensional probability. Select those needed for your question. Do not treat all as compulsory for entry-level systematic research.

### 4.2 Statistics and empirical methodology

**Core:** likelihood, estimators, bias and variance, consistency, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, Bayesian updating, linear/logistic regression, regularization, bootstrap, residual diagnostics, and experimental design.

**Graduate bridge:** sufficiency; Fisher information; estimator asymptotics; likelihood-ratio tests; delta method; concentration and uniform convergence; nonparametric estimation; multiple comparisons; dependence-aware uncertainty estimates.

**Finance-specific application:** chronological validation, overlapping labels, purging observations with overlapping information intervals, justified embargo/gaps, survivorship bias, publication lags, corporate actions, data revisions, risk exposures, transaction costs, and the uncertainty of performance estimates.

Different splitting rules address different problems. Ordinary time-series splitting preserves time order; it does not automatically remove all overlap or ensure point-in-time data correctness. Scikit-learn explicitly warns that inappropriate cross-validation can train on future observations and test on the past. [TimeSeriesSplit documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.model_selection.TimeSeriesSplit.html).

### 4.3 ML and time series

Start with linear models, ridge/lasso, trees, gradient boosting, model selection, and calibration. Then study autocorrelation, stationarity, AR/MA/ARIMA, volatility models, state-space models, Lọc Kalman, hidden Markov models, and online learning.

Graduate additions should include generalization, regularization, empirical risk minimization, concentration-based reasoning, probabilistic modeling, uncertainty estimation, and dịch chuyển phân phối. Neural networks are an optional method within a controlled comparison; they are not the default baseline.

Your robotics advantage should become visible in a project about inference or sequential decisions. Learning a Kalman filter well enough to derive and diagnose it is more valuable than adding five agent frameworks to your CV.

### 4.4 Programming and computing

**Python:** NumPy, a dataframe library, SciPy, statistical/ML libraries, plotting, SQL, environments, profiling, logging, and reproducible command-line experiments. Learn Python early even though C++ is already familiar.

**C++:** standard containers, complexity, memory ownership, debugging, profiling, floating-point pitfalls, tests, and efficient numerical routines. Add concurrency and low-latency techniques if your track needs them.

**Research engineering:** immutable data snapshots; recorded code versions; deterministic configurations; testable transformations; unit and timestamp consistency; experiment IDs; metrics with uncertainty; and a documented replay path.

**Algorithms:** arrays, strings, sorting, binary search, hashing, heaps, graph traversal, dynamic programming, and complexity. Use Codeforces as practice, not the central research credential.

### 4.5 Financial knowledge

Learn returns versus prices, compounding, excess returns, equities, ETFs, futures, options, order types, spreads, liquidity, leverage, margin, shorting, borrow costs, and P&L accounting.

Then cover factor models, portfolio risk, covariance estimation, diversification, constrained allocation, turnover, market impact, execution, capacity, and asset-pricing intuition.

For derivatives, add arbitrage, replication, risk-neutral valuation, binomial models, Black–Scholes, Greeks, volatility surfaces, calibration, and numerical pricing. Risk-neutral pricing probabilities and real-world return forecasting probabilities serve different purposes.

### 4.6 Communication and judgment

Write one concise technical memo monthly. Give a 10–15-minute presentation at least quarterly. Learn to state a hypothesis, identify assumptions, defend an inference, report a failed experiment, and explain why a model is operationally unsuitable despite a good offline score.

Maintain an error log for mathematics and an experiment log for research. Both should distinguish a mistaken assumption from a coding defect or a genuinely negative result.

## 5. The 24-month execution plan

The dates below assume a start in October 2026. Course overlap with your degree should reduce duplicated work. Keep at most **two serious taught subjects plus one project** active at a time; the monthly entries sequence topics within that limit.

### Months 1–3: October–December 2026 — foundations and scientific programming

**Month 1:** Run the diagnostic. Repair calculus/linear algebra gaps. Begin scientific Python, Git, environments, and testing. Translate a few familiar C++ tasks into Python and implement numerical routines. Identify faculty working in statistics, ML, control, optimization, or time series.

**Month 2:** Study conditional probability, distributions, moments, and elementary inference. Implement OLS using a numerically stable decomposition; compare it with a trusted library. Use simulations to distinguish correlation from independence and sampling noise from model error.

**Month 3:** Continue probability and proof writing. Study eigenvalues/SVD and PCA. Complete a small Monte Carlo project on estimation or sampling uncertainty. Prepare a two-page technical memo and start attending a relevant research seminar.

**Deliverables:** a foundations repository, worked problem sets, an error log, and one reproducible simulation report. Do not advertise toy simulations as profitable trading strategies.

**Gate:** Independently derive and implement least squares, reason through unfamiliar conditional-probability problems, and explain what your simulator validates.

### Months 4–6: January–March 2027 — inference and first financial experiment

**Month 4:** Study estimation, likelihood, confidence intervals, and hypothesis testing. Continue real-analysis/proof foundations. Learn financial returns, excess returns, factor exposures, and basic P&L accounting.

**Month 5:** Study regression, regularization, bootstrap, and diagnostics. Start a factor-regression replication using the Kenneth French Data Library. Record which data vintage and definitions you used. Factor returns are research portfolios, not automatically executable investment products.

**Month 6:** Compare expanding/rolling estimation windows. Assess residual dependence and choose defensible uncertainty estimates. Produce a four-to-six-page replication memo. Seek a supervised summer project or research assistantship; apply to appropriate early-career internships.

**Deliverables:** your first finance replication, a one-page CV, and a clear short description of the research interests you want to pursue.

**Gate:** You can explain the difference between predicting an outcome and estimating a causal effect; interpret uncertainty honestly; and rebuild the report from documented inputs. [Kenneth French Data Library](https://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/faculty/ken.french/data_library.html).

### Months 7–9: April–June 2027 — optimization, time series, and a competition

**Month 7:** Begin convex optimization and time-series fundamentals. Solve a regularized regression or constrained quadratic allocation problem. Explain how poor covariance estimation can make a mathematically optimal allocation unstable.

**Month 8:** Implement AR-style baselines, a simple volatility forecast, and a basic Kalman filter on synthetic data. Validate the filter on a known data-generating process before applying it to financial data.

**Month 9:** Enter one suitable competition if its new edition is available and you are eligible. Treat competition preparation as the project for these weeks. Otherwise use an archived financial forecasting challenge. Finalize arrangements for summer research or an internship.

**Deliverables:** an optimization notebook or package, a chronological-validation harness, and a competition/project postmortem.

**Gate:** All preprocessing is fitted only on allowed training observations; forecasts precede target realization; and a simple baseline is present. If you cannot verify those properties, stop tuning models and repair the pipeline.

### Months 10–12: July–September 2027 — supervised work and graduate-course entry

**Month 10:** Work in an RA position, technical internship, or supervised project. Focus on a scoped question with a measurable deliverable. Start the bridge toward measure-based probability only if the earlier gate passed.

**Month 11:** Begin graduate statistical inference. Derive selected likelihood/asymptotic results and connect them to simulation. Use your supervisor's feedback to choose one second-year research direction.

**Month 12:** Finish the supervised deliverable and present it. Sit a self-administered assessment using unseen undergraduate/graduate-bridge problems. Identify next year's internships by their actual graduation-year requirements.

**Deliverables:** supervisor feedback, a second technical report, and a month-12 skills audit.

**Gate:** You can explain a research result without reading a notebook and answer questions about its assumptions, validation, failure modes, and missing evidence. If probability remains weak, postpone an advanced elective rather than rushing it.

### Months 13–15: October–December 2027 — graduate probability and theoretical statistics

**Month 13:** Continue rigorous probability: measurable variables, expectation, convergence, and interchange of limits/integration. Use graduate course problem sets as the standard.

**Month 14:** Study graduate inference: concentration, consistency, likelihood methods, asymptotic normality, and the delta method. Tie theoretical statements to small simulations that demonstrate when their assumptions matter.

**Month 15:** Produce a literature map for your specialization. Read approximately 8–12 central papers carefully, distinguishing seminal methods, empirical comparisons, and unresolved questions. Draft a replication protocol before looking at final held-out results.

**Deliverables:** graduate problem sets and a replication proposal reviewed by a lecturer, PhD student, or researcher.

**Gate:** You can state the assumptions of a theorem before using it and distinguish convergence in probability, distribution, and stronger modes. Progress on selected subjects is the goal; this does not cover an entire statistics PhD first year.

### Months 16–18: January–March 2028 — advanced ML and serious replication

**Month 16:** Study generalization, regularization, online learning, and dịch chuyển phân phối. Finish a faithful replication of one method on an accessible dataset.

**Month 17:** Perform ablations and sensitivity tests. Compare a zero/naive predictor, a linear model, and your selected advanced method. Account for dependence and the number of variants tried.

**Month 18:** Write a replication report describing both agreement and disagreement with the source. Agree on one narrow original extension with your supervisor. Interview for research or technical summer opportunities if eligible.

**Deliverables:** a clean replication repository, a technical report, and a pre-specified extension plan.

**Gate:** A second person can rerun your central result; you can explain whether a difference from the paper comes from data, implementation, protocol, or scientific uncertainty.

### Months 19–21: April–June 2028 — original extension

**Month 19:** Freeze the principal hypothesis, baselines, main metric, temporal split, and experiment budget. Implement the extension. Keep a truly unseen evaluation period if the dataset permits it.

**Month 20:** Evaluate across multiple chronological windows, random seeds where relevant, and realistic operational constraints. Examine stability, uncertainty, costs, and model failure.

**Month 21:** Write a manuscript draft. Ask for adversarial technical review: where can the result be leakage, omitted exposure, overfitting, poor measurement, or an unfair comparison? Run only revisions justified by that review and record the expanded search.

**Deliverables:** a substantial manuscript draft, an experiment registry, and reviewer comments.

**Gate:** Your claimed contribution survives fair baselines and a documented audit. A non-improvement can still produce a useful paper or thesis if it resolves a meaningful question rigorously.

### Months 22–24: July–September 2028 — assessment, presentation, and next step

**Month 22:** Complete a summer RA/internship or consolidate the supervised extension. Explain what changed because of external feedback.

**Month 23:** Finalize the manuscript, limitations, data documentation, and reproduction instructions. Present to a lab, student research meeting, or appropriate workshop. Submission is optional and should depend on mentor assessment and genuine novelty.

**Month 24:** Conduct a two-part assessment: written problems in selected graduate subjects, plus an oral defense of your research. Seek an external reviewer. Decide whether to deepen research, pursue a research master's after graduation, apply for eligible internships, or prepare for later doctoral applications.

**Deliverables:** a research portfolio, reviewed manuscript, recorded/presented technical talk, skills audit, and an application strategy.

**Gate:** You independently solve representative problems at the chosen graduate-course level and defend the research design. Do not claim that a self-administered examination certifies you as PhD-qualified.

## 6. Weekly workload and adjustment rules

During term, start with **18–22 focused hours per week beyond ordinary coursework**, reducing this if the degree already has a heavy load. Count degree modules toward the roadmap where they overlap. A 25-hour stretch schedule is appropriate only if it is sustainable; during exams, reduce the additional workload. An internship replaces the project workload rather than being added on top.

| Period | Theory/problem solving | Research/building | Coding/interviews | Papers/writing/mentor | Total extra hours |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Months 1–6 | 9 | 6 | 3 | 2 | 20 |
| Months 7–12 | 8 | 7 | 3 | 2 | 20 |
| Months 13–18 | 8 | 9 | 2 | 3 | 22 |
| Months 19–24 | 5 | 12 | 2 | 3 | 22 |

Suggested rhythm: four weekday sessions of 90 minutes for theory; two weekday sessions of 60 minutes for coding or review; two weekend blocks of four hours for research; one two-hour writing/mentor block; and an optional two-hour revision block. Reallocate rather than adding tasks when a competition is active.

Track completed problems and defended results, not lecture giờ. A useful self-imposed course gate is about 75% correct on a representative unseen assessment plus a satisfactory explanation of the key errors. This threshold is a planning aid, not a university pass mark.

If two consecutive monthly reviews show unresolved foundations or slipping degree performance, drop an elective or competition. If supervised work expands, reduce course breadth. At 10–12 extra hours per week, aim for undergraduate mastery, one graduate subject, and one serious project in two years; retain the rest for a later stage.

## 7. Curated resources: use one main source per subject

| Subject | Primary resource | When and how to use it |
|---|---|---|
| Linear algebra | [MIT 18.06, Gilbert Strang](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06-linear-algebra-spring-2010/) | Months 1–3; solve exercises and an unseen exam; supplement with stable least-squares implementations |
| Probability | [Harvard Stat 110, Blitzstein and Hwang](https://stat110.hsites.harvard.edu/) | Months 1–6; full problem-solving course, not just videos; the official site links a free book |
| Proofs/analysis | [Lebl, Basic Analysis, free online text](https://www.jirka.org/ra/) | Months 2–8 as needed; use the free author-hosted text and proof exercises |
| Introductory statistical ML | [An Introduction to Statistical Learning, Python edition](https://www.statlearning.com/) | Months 4–9; complete labs and derive simple models; official book downloads available |
| Statistical inference bridge | [MIT 18.05 public inference readings](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/pages/classes-reading-and-in-class-materials/) | Months 4–12; free notes, problems, and solutions for inference; use CMU 36-705 public notes for bootstrap and advanced estimation |
| Graduate theoretical statistics | [CMU 36-705, public notes](https://stat.cmu.edu/~siva/teaching/705/) | Months 11–18; probability prerequisites first; solve proof-based exercises |
| Graduate probability | [MIT 6.436J Fundamentals of Probability](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-436j-fundamentals-of-probability-fall-2018/pages/lecture-notes/) | Months 10–18; rigorous graduate bridge; course assumes elementary probability and mathematical maturity |
| Optimization | [Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization](https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/cvxbook/) | Months 7–15; core convexity, optimality, duality, and selected numerical algorithms; free official PDF |
| Time series | [Hyndman and Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice](https://otexts.com/fpp3/) | Months 7–12; forecast evaluation and classical methods; this edition uses R, so translate selected ideas to Python |
| Advanced ML | [Hastie, Tibshirani, Friedman, Elements of Statistical Learning](https://hastie.su.domains/ElemStatLearn/main.html) | Months 13–18; selected chapters after ISL; official author-hosted book |
| Market structure | [CME Institute free courses and market mechanics](https://www.cmegroup.com/education) | Months 5–12; free futures/market mechanics lessons, Investor.gov order types, and MIT 18.S096 market lectures; this introductory bundle is not a complete advanced microstructure textbook |
| Derivatives alternative | [Xi Geng, CMU free stochastic-calculus notes](https://www.math.cmu.edu/~xig/Stochastic%20Calculus%20%28Fall%202016%29.html) | Selected material in year 2 only if pricing/control is the chosen track; graduate/master's finance material, not proof of PhD equivalence |

A finance research overview for year 2 is [Kelly and Xiu, Financial Machine Learning](https://bfi.uchicago.edu/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/BFI_WP_2023-100.pdf). The backtesting methodology reading is [Bailey et al., The Probability of Backtest Overfitting](https://www.davidhbailey.com/dhbpapers/backtest-prob.pdf). Read these to identify research problems and failure modes; do not expect a survey or a single backtesting statistic to replace methodological judgment.

Mọi tài liệu học tập và nghiên cứu bắt buộc đều phải miễn phí. Xem the public full-text books, university notes, and open working papers linked here. No paid textbook, certificate, journal access, institutional subscription, dataset, LLM API, or rented GPU is required. Paper selection must include a free full-text/access check and a local CPU feasibility pilot. See the Obsidian Free Resources and Access Policy for direct links, topic routing, and project fallbacks.

## 8. Build three substantial projects

### Project A: inference and factor-model replication — months 4–6

**Question:** How stable are estimated market and factor exposures across time, and how does uncertainty change when returns are dependent?

**Data:** Kenneth French factors and research portfolios, with documented units and data vintage.

**Methods:** OLS, rolling/expanding estimation, residual diagnostics, appropriate heteroskedasticity/autocorrelation-aware uncertainty, and a comparison with a simple benchmark.

**Output:** a short report, reproducible code, data dictionary, and limitations. Distinguish contemporaneous explanatory regressions from genuine forecasts. Do not count a contemporaneous factor fit as a trading signal.

### Project B: chronological financial forecasting — months 7–12

Use one archived challenge: [Jane Street Real-Time Market Data Forecasting](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/jane-street-real-time-market-data-forecasting/data) or [Optiver Trading at the Close](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/optiver-trading-at-the-close). Both competitions have finished; they are practice resources, subject to their data-use rules. [Jane Street final leaderboard](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/jane-street-real-time-market-data-forecasting/leaderboard), [Optiver final leaderboard](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/optiver-trading-at-the-close/leaderboard).

**Compare:** zero/naive forecasts, ridge regression, a boosting model, and a sequential model only when justified. Use chronological windows, fitting all transformations within each training window. Group observations by time when assets share information; do not randomly scatter the same market period between training and validation.

**Evaluate:** the official forecasting metric, stability across time segments, sensitivity to missing data, and inference cost. An anonymized prediction score does not establish a tradable strategy or net profitability. Without interpretable prices and an execution model, do not manufacture a P&L claim.

**Output:** a validation harness, model comparison, and failure analysis. Because these datasets and winning solutions are already public, disclose what you read; an untouched local holdout cannot erase prior exposure to published results.

### Project C: supervised sequential-learning extension — months 13–24

Suggested question: **When do adaptive state-space or online linear models improve forecast calibration under dịch chuyển phân phối, compared with fixed and rolling-window baselines?**

Start on synthetic data where latent states and changes are known, then use one real dataset. Select one outcome—such as volatility or an anonymized forecasting target—and one principal metric. Prediction intervals for heteroskedastic/dependent data require care; do not use an IID calibration claim without justification.

**Protocol:** replicate a published baseline; define the extension; evaluate multiple chronological windows; examine model components with ablations; estimate uncertainty with methods suited to dependence; record every tested variant. Explain the mechanism and compute requirements, not just the best number.

**Potential contribution:** a better method, a narrower operating regime where an existing method works, a reliable replication that challenges a claim, or a rigorous benchmark identifying failure. A mentor should assess whether the work is suitable for a thesis, workshop, or publication.

If good event-level data and an execution supervisor are available, an alternative is uncertainty-aware inventory/execution control. If pricing is the chosen track, replace Project C with pricing/hedging/calibration research and add the relevant stochastic/numerical coursework.

## 9. Use agentic workflows in a way researchers can trust

An appropriate workflow is:

**Versioned literature sources → explicit hypothesis → timestamped data snapshot → fixed experiment configuration → chronological validation → complete experiment log → reviewed report.**

Build agents that retrieve and summarize papers with source links; check data schemas; generate small reviewed code changes; run pre-specified experiments; flag suspicious timestamps; and draft figures or reports from verified results.

Keep an immutable record of all search attempts and model variants. Agents must not quietly retune on a held-out set, invent citations, alter data definitions, or present a selected winning run as the only experiment conducted. Automated search increases the importance of multiple-testing and selection control. [Backtest overfitting research](https://www.davidhbailey.com/dhbpapers/backtest-prob.pdf).

LLM-assisted historical financial prediction introduces another issue: a model trained later can contain information about historical outcomes, even when the documents supplied in the prompt are timestamp-correct. If you cannot establish temporal validity of the model itself, restrict it to engineering assistance or qualify historical forecasting conclusions explicitly. Recent research examines point-in-time language-model evaluation directly. [Scaling Point-in-Time Language Models, free arXiv full text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11889).

Measure your workflow by reproduction success, auditability, detection of defects, and researcher time saved—not by number of agents.

## 10. Which work experience to prioritize

For the two-year academic goal, evaluate opportunities by mentor quality, technical responsibility, access to data, and the research result you can explain afterward.

| Role | Why it helps | Suitable timing | What to inspect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Faculty RA in statistics, ML, control, optimization, econometrics | Builds research habits and a detailed reference | Seek from months 3–6; deepen in months 10–24 | Regular supervision; ownership of a question; serious experiments |
| Quantitative research intern | Direct signal/model research and finance feedback | Apply when requirements and readiness fit, usually after first substantial project | Degree stage; graduation year; research versus support work |
| ML research / data-science intern | Transferable inference and empirical modeling | Months 6–24 | Model validation, time series, experiment design, and mentoring |
| Research engineer / quant developer intern | Builds research infrastructure and model implementation | Months 6–24 | Contact with researchers and ownership beyond maintenance |
| C++/Python software intern | Improves production engineering and technical discipline | Useful first summer option | Real code review, tests, profiling, numerical/data work |
| Bank quant / model-validation intern | Gives modeling, derivatives, and risk experience | Often later undergraduate/graduate stages | Mathematical depth; validation versus administrative reporting |
| General finance, sales, or unrelated automation work | Provides workplace experience, but fewer direct research skills | Backup based on personal circumstances | Whether the actual work adds technical evidence |

For you, a robotics/ML RA studying uncertainty or sequential learning can be more useful than a finance-labelled internship with little modeling. Conversely, a well-supervised research-engineering internship can be excellent even if it is not called quantitative research.

### Examples of firms and role titles

- **Citadel:** Quantitative Research Analyst Intern, including BS/MS tracks. [Example Europe posting](https://www.citadel.com/careers/details/quantitative-research-analyst-intern-bs-ms-europe/).
- **Jane Street:** Quantitative Researcher Internship, involving market data, models, and strategies. [Example research internship](https://www.janestreet.com/join-jane-street/position/8498547002/).
- **HRT:** Algorithm Development Internship; research-oriented despite the title. The current Summer 2027 student listing is for 2028 graduates and includes NYC, London, and Singapore. [Student opportunities](https://www.hudsonrivertrading.com/student-opportunities/).
- **Optiver:** Quantitative Research Internship at selected offices; undergraduate and PhD pathways exist, with specific postings controlling eligibility. [Research internship overview](https://www.optiver.com/join-us/students/internships/research/).
- **Two Sigma:** Quantitative research internships and campus researcher opportunities. [Careers](https://www.twosigma.com/careers/).
- **WorldQuant:** research, quant development, and BRAIN research pathways. The live board includes Vietnam research and WQBRAIN AI research roles; they should not be presumed to be student internships. A recently indexed Vietnam internship titled “Quantitative Research Intern (LLMs & AI Agents)” fits your background, but its direct listing redirected to the general board when checked. Treat it as a role type to watch, not a verified open vacancy. [Live WorldQuant board](https://job-boards.greenhouse.io/worldquant).

Relocation flexibility expands the search; it does not establish work authorization. Record office, eligibility, graduation date, sponsorship language, application status, and role substance for each posting. Do not relocate simply to compensate for missing foundational preparation.

### Recruiting calendar and application process

For summer internships, begin checking official postings in the preceding summer and keep checking through autumn/winter; opening dates differ by firm, office, and year. Do not infer next year's deadlines from last year's schedule. Prepare your CV and first technical report before the cycle you are eligible for.

The current HRT page illustrates why graduation year matters: an excellent first-year candidate expecting to graduate in 2030 does not meet a listing restricted to 2028 graduates. Some early-student programs have separate routes. Early in this plan, faculty research and broadly accessible technical internships may therefore be the practical priorities.

Maintain a focused list of employers and laboratories. Apply to roles where the requirements fit; tailor your project description to the research question. A CV bullet should state your contribution, validation, and result, for example: “Compared rolling and state-space forecasts across chronological evaluation windows; quantified performance uncertainty and documented sensitivity to changing regimes.” Use actual measurements, not invented claims.

For faculty outreach, read one paper and propose a small contribution. Example: “I am a robotics/AI undergraduate interested in sequential inference. I read your paper on [topic] and built [relevant small replication]. Could I contribute to a scoped replication or experiment for 6–8 hours per week?” This is a template to send yourself, not a message sent on your behalf.

## 11. Competitions: prioritize learning and access

Aim for **one finance/data competition and one programming/mathematics activity per year**, with no more than one intensive competition at a time. A serious competition should produce a codebase and postmortem. Do not sacrifice the supervised project merely to collect participation badges.

| Opportunity | Recommended priority | What it develops | Eligibility/status checked on 7 Oct 2026 |
|---|---|---|---|
| IMC Prosperity | High for market-making/trading exploration | Python algorithms, inventory management, simulated markets, teamwork | Prosperity 4 ran Apr 14–30, 2026; teams up to 5. Learning participation is broader than prize eligibility. 2027 dates not assumed. [Official page](https://prosperity.imc.com/) |
| WorldQuant BRAIN IQC | High if interested in equity signals | Alpha construction, cross-sectional ideas, platform-based experiments | 2026 qualifier began Mar 17 and has passed. Teams 1–4; age 18+; institution and prior-affiliation restrictions. 2027 rules not assumed. [Official rules/FAQ](https://www.worldquant.com/brain/iqc/) |
| Citadel/Correlation One Datathons | High when your cohort is eligible | Data analysis, inference, teamwork, presentations | Region/cohort-specific. Current Asia/APAC page lists graduation Dec 2026–Jun 2028; a 2030 graduate would not fit this edition. [Official eligibility](https://www.citadel.com/careers/programs-and-events/datathons/) |
| Kaggle financial forecasting | High as research practice | Forecast validation, noisy data, model comparison | Jane Street Real-Time Market Data Forecasting and Optiver Trading at the Close are completed events; use as archived exercises under their rules. New events have their own eligibility. [Competition directory](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions) |
| ICPC / Codeforces | Medium, ongoing | Algorithms, debugging, teamwork, interview fluency | ICPC involves university teams and season-specific eligibility; use your university coach/current regional rules. [ICPC](https://icpc.global/) |
| UChicago Trading Competition | High if accessible during early undergraduate years | Algorithmic trading, options, market making | 2026 event ran Apr 10–11; freshmen/sophomores only, 3–4 students, at least one Python programmer; selection required. Do not assume unchanged 2027 rules. [Application rules](https://tradingcompetition.uchicago.edu/application.html) |
| Rotman International Trading Competition | Optional; excellent if institution supports a team | Simulated decision cases and trading under pressure | 2027 event advertised Feb 18–20; registration page says stay tuned. One university team, four student members, current undergraduate/graduate enrolment. [Event](https://ritc.rotman.utoronto.ca/), [registration rules](https://www.rotman.utoronto.ca/faculty-and-research/education-labs/bmo-financial-group-finance-research-and-trading-lab/rotman-international-trading-competition/registration/) |
| International Mathematics Competition for University Students | Optional if mathematical problem solving is a strength | Proofs and advanced undergraduate reasoning | Distinct from IMC Trading; 2026 materials target students completing years 1–4. Arrange participation and funding through your institution. [Official site](https://imc-math.org.uk/) |
| Putnam | Optional and region-limited | Proof-based undergraduate problem solving | Dec 5, 2026; enrolled at an institution in US/Canada/Mexico; no prior bachelor's; at most four official participations. Foreign nationality itself is not exclusion. [MAA eligibility](https://maa.org/putnam/) |

Two details materially affect planning:

1. **IMC Prosperity 4 prizes:** its listed prize regions exclude Vietnam and Singapore, although broader learning/leaderboard participation is possible. Check the future edition separately. Current or accepted employment at IMC or certain competing trading firms also affects eligibility. [Prosperity rules](https://prosperity.imc.com/).
2. **IQC 2026 exclusions:** BRAIN consultant status and certain previous employment, competition, or WorldQuant University affiliations can affect eligibility. Choosing a consultant pathway may change which competition edition you can enter. Participation, prizes, consultant work, internships, and full-time employment are different outcomes. [IQC FAQ](https://www.worldquant.com/brain/iqc/).

### Your competition preparation

For Codeforces, spend roughly 2–3 hours per week initially: learn binary search, prefix sums, two pointers, greedy reasoning, basic graph traversal, and dynamic programming; enter contests and upsolve mistakes. Move gradually into unfamiliar 1100–1400-level tasks. Later explore 1400–1600 tasks if this still improves your coding. Ratings are optional progress indicators, not QR hiring thresholds.

For Prosperity, prepare Python, order-book terminology, positions, cash/P&L, simple quoting rules, and risk limits. For IQC, learn ranking, neutralization, turnover, signal correlation, and why large expression searches create selection bias. For datathons/Kaggle, practice cleaning, baselines, temporal validation, uncertainty, and clear short presentations.

## 12. Interview preparation

Begin light practice after the foundations; intensify only before actual eligible applications. Use four parallel skill areas:

1. **Probability:** conditioning, expectation, distributions, combinatorics, Markov chains, and simulation checks.
2. **Statistics/research:** estimation, regression, uncertainty, overfitting, dependence, model comparison, and explanation of your own work.
3. **Coding:** common structures/algorithms, readable implementations, complexity, edge cases, and numerical correctness.
4. **Communication:** think aloud, state assumptions, take feedback, and explain technical choices.

Jane Street provides an official Probability & Markets guide. Citadel's campus research process explicitly discusses programming, research ability, data structures/algorithms, and problem-solving. These support broad preparation; no single interview format should define your entire curriculum. [Jane Street guide](https://www.janestreet.com/probability-markets/), [Citadel research interviews](https://www.citadel.com/careers/career-perspectives/our-quantitative-research-interview-process/).

Luyện one technical mock per month from month 7, increasing frequency around applications. Give a five-minute summary of your project followed by questions such as: What was known at prediction time? How many variants did you try? What would falsify the result? Which baseline was hardest to beat? Why might it fail after deployment?

Fast mental arithmetic and puzzle speed can matter for some trading roles. For research preparation, do not let them displace inference, programming, or empirical work.

## 13. What the final portfolio should contain

Keep three or four polished repositories, not a large collection of unfinished demos:

- Foundations/simulation work demonstrating understanding of estimation and numerical methods.
- Factor or forecasting replication with careful validation and a short technical report.
- A supervised extension with a manuscript and reproduction instructions.
- Optional research-workflow tooling that directly supports the above work.

Each major repository needs a question; data source and permitted use; code/data version; setup instructions; baselines; evaluation protocol; complete principal results; ablations; limitations; and a concise account of your contribution. Publish only material you have permission to share.

For any tradable strategy claim, also describe information availability, position timing, costs, turnover, exposure, drawdown, capacity assumptions, and uncertainty. For forecasting-only projects, report forecasting results and explain the missing bridge to trading.

Do not list “PhD-level quant researcher” as a self-awarded CV title. List the actual advanced subjects studied, research contribution, supervisor, and evidence.

## 14. After month 24: continue toward expertise

If this plan begins in your first undergraduate year, you will likely still be completing the degree after two years. Use the remaining university years for advanced electives, a strong thesis, eligible research internships, and sustained supervision. Self-study does not override admission requirements for a completed degree or equivalent qualification.

Three useful later routes are:

| Route | Choose it when | Main decision criterion |
|---|---|---|
| Bachelor's → research role | You obtain a genuine modeling/research position with strong mentoring | Quality of work and team, not title alone |
| Bachelor's → research master's → industry or doctorate | You need stronger mathematics, research exposure, or a bridge to new laboratories/regions | Supervisor, thesis opportunity, placement, funding, and total cost |
| Bachelor's → PhD in statistics/ML/applied math/OR/CS/econometrics | You enjoy original research and have strong academic/research evidence | Advisor fit, funding, and research environment |

A finance-branded degree is not mandatory for all QR roles. A quantitatively rigorous degree with substantial research can align well with employer requirements. A PhD is valuable when its training and research match your interests; it should not be treated as an automatic route to a trading job.

Expertise develops through repeated responsibility for research decisions: identifying worthwhile questions, rejecting spurious results, understanding economic mechanisms, handling deployment and changing data, and learning from failure. That record takes additional years and cannot be scheduled with the same certainty as a course syllabus.

## 15. Immediate actions

1. In the next two weeks, complete the mathematics diagnostic and have representative solutions checked.
2. Choose one probability resource and one linear-algebra/proof resource based on the diagnostic.
3. Establish a sustainable 20-hour weekly schedule with no more than two serious courses plus one project.
4. Build an OLS/Monte Carlo foundations repository before building a trading agent.
5. Identify five relevant faculty/labs; read a paper from the most promising two and seek a small supervised contribution.
6. Track competition editions and internship eligibility, especially graduation-year and region restrictions.
7. At the end of each quarter, assess unseen problem-solving, a reproducible artifact, and external feedback; change the next quarter's scope based on that evidence.

body:
# Plan decisions and provenance

Prepared 7 October 2026 from the user's robotics/AI background, agentic-workflow specialty, C++ Codeforces experience, and requested two-year quant-research roadmap.

The user specified **four hours per day, five days per week**. The weekday selection defaults to Monday–Friday. Start defaults to 2026-10-07; end is 2028-10-06. There are 731 calendar notes, including weekend rest notes. Months are rolling calendar months anchored on the start date; curriculum weeks run Wednesday–Tuesday and the final module is partial.

The 105 topic modules and task durations are proposed planning decisions, not institutional requirements. Future research methods, experiments, publication dates, and opportunities depend on evidence and supervision. See the original roadmap for researched academic/career sources. Resource notes link primary sources; content is not copied from copyrighted textbooks.

Obsidian uses native Markdown task lists, linked notes, search, and an enabled Bases core plugin. No third-party plugin or global Daily Notes setting is required or changed. Official format references: https://help.obsidian.md/bases/syntax and https://help.obsidian.md/bases/functions .

The user additionally requires all resources and research materials to be free. Applied 7 October 2026: paid textbook recommendations were replaced; papers use open full-text links; local-compute feasibility and free-data alternatives are required. See [[Road to Quant/Free Resources and Access Policy]].

# Quyết định lập kế hoạch và nguồn gốc

Lập ngày 7 tháng 10 năm 2026, dựa trên nền tảng robot học/AI, chuyên môn quy trình tác tử, kinh nghiệm C++ trên Codeforces và yêu cầu xây dựng lộ trình nghiên cứu định lượng trong hai năm.

Người dùng chọn **bốn giờ mỗi ngày, năm ngày mỗi tuần**. Mặc định làm việc từ thứ Hai đến thứ Sáu. Ngày bắt đầu là 2026-10-07; kết thúc 2028-10-06. Có 731 ghi chú theo lịch, gồm cả ghi chú nghỉ cuối tuần. Tháng được tính tuần tự từ ngày bắt đầu; tuần học chạy từ thứ Tư đến thứ Ba và mô-đun cuối cùng không trọn tuần.

105 mô-đun chủ đề và thời lượng công việc là đề xuất lập kế hoạch, không phải yêu cầu của trường. Phương pháp nghiên cứu, thí nghiệm, ngày phát hành và cơ hội trong tương lai phụ thuộc vào minh chứng và sự hướng dẫn. Xem lộ trình gốc để biết nguồn học thuật/nghề nghiệp đã tra cứu. Ghi chú tài liệu dẫn tới nguồn gốc; nội dung không sao chép từ giáo trình có bản quyền.

Obsidian dùng danh sách việc cần làm Markdown, ghi chú liên kết, tìm kiếm và tiện ích Bases có sẵn đã bật. Không cần cài tiện ích bên thứ ba hay thay đổi thiết lập Daily Notes toàn cục. Tài liệu định dạng chính thức: https://help.obsidian.md/bases/syntax và https://help.obsidian.md/bases/functions .

Người dùng cũng yêu cầu mọi tài liệu và tư liệu nghiên cứu đều miễn phí. Áp dụng từ ngày 7 tháng 10 năm 2026: thay sách trả phí bằng tài liệu miễn phí; liên kết bài báo tới toàn văn mở; yêu cầu kiểm tra khả năng chạy trên máy cá nhân và dùng dữ liệu miễn phí. Xem [[Road to Quant/Free Resources and Access Policy]].

# Road to Quant — start here

**Plan:** 2026-10-07 through 2028-10-06 (24 calendar months, 731 daily notes). **Schedule:** four hours Monday–Friday; weekends free. **Target:** selected graduate-level competence and supervised research readiness.

## Today

![[Road to Quant/Daily Navigator.base#Today]]

Open the date in the table and tick its individual tasks. The table uses the installed Obsidian Bases core plugin and the computer's current date. Set the daily note's `status` to `done` after completion; checkbox completion does not automatically change that property.

**First day:** [[Road to Quant/Daily/2026-10/2026-10-07|2026-10-07]]. **If the table is unavailable:** use the month calendars below or Quick Switcher (Ctrl+O) and type the date.

## Next seven days

![[Road to Quant/Daily Navigator.base#Next seven days]]

## Use the plan

1. Open today's note and work through its four-hour block.
2. Store code and reports in the named project; paste evidence links into the daily note.
3. On the last weekday of each module, complete the weekly review inside the allocated time.
4. At each monthly gate, adapt later notes to actual progress and semester workload.
5. Use [[Road to Quant/Recovery and Adjustment Rules]] after interruptions; do not stack missed work.

The complete calendar is a proposed sequence, not a prediction of learning speed. Coursework and internship overlap replace relevant blocks. Quarterly gates determine whether advanced modules need postponing. No daily reminder automation or public GitHub upload has been created.

**Lộ trình:** 2026-10-07 through 2028-10-06 (24 tháng theo lịch, 731 ghi chú hằng ngày). **Lịch học:** bốn giờ từ thứ Hai đến thứ Sáu; nghỉ cuối tuần. **Mục tiêu:** nắm vững một số nội dung trình độ sau đại học và sẵn sàng làm nghiên cứu có hướng dẫn.

## Hôm nay

![[Road to Quant/Daily Navigator.base#Today]]

Mở ngày trong bảng rồi đánh dấu từng việc. Bảng dùng tiện ích Bases có sẵn của Obsidian và ngày hiện tại trên máy tính. Sau khi hoàn thành, hãy đổi `status` của ghi chú ngày thành `done`; đánh dấu checkbox không tự đổi thuộc tính đó.

**Ngày đầu tiên:** [[Road to Quant/Daily/2026-10/2026-10-07|2026-10-07]]. **Nếu bảng không hiển thị:** dùng lịch tháng bên dưới hoặc Quick Switcher (Ctrl+O) rồi nhập ngày.

## Bảy ngày tiếp theo

![[Road to Quant/Daily Navigator.base#Next seven days]]

## Cách sử dụng lộ trình

1. Mở ghi chú hôm nay và làm theo khối công việc bốn giờ.
2. Lưu mã nguồn và báo cáo trong dự án tương ứng; dán liên kết minh chứng vào ghi chú ngày.
3. Vào ngày làm việc cuối của mỗi mô-đun, hoàn tất phần tổng kết tuần trong thời gian đã phân bổ.

5. Dùng [[Road to Quant/Recovery and Adjustment Rules]] sau khi bị gián đoạn; đừng dồn việc đã bỏ lỡ vào ngày sau.

Lịch đầy đủ là trình tự đề xuất, không dự đoán tốc độ học của bạn. Khi trùng lịch học ở trường hoặc thực tập, hãy dùng thời gian đó thay cho khối công việc liên quan. # Week 2: Vectors and probability spaces

[[Road to Quant/START HERE|Dashboard]] · [[Road to Quant/Projects/P01|quant-foundations-lab]]

**Window:** 2026-10-14–2026-10-20. **Budget:** 20 hours; weekends are free.

**Study:** vector spaces, linear independence, sample spaces, and event algebra.

**Derive / solve:** construct bases for two subspaces and enumerate outcomes for two finite probability models.

**Build:** implement vector projections and a finite-outcome probability calculator.

**Experiment:** check projection residual orthogonality and exact versus simulated probabilities.

**Evidence:** vectors-and-events.md with two derivations and reproducible examples.

**Resources:** [[Road to Quant/Resources/LA|LA]], [[Road to Quant/Resources/PROB|PROB]].

**Window:** 2027-02-03–2027-02-09. **Budget:** 20 hours; weekends are free.

**Study:** null hypotheses, power, p-values, effect sizes, and practical significance.

**Build:** implement hypothesis-test simulations and factor coefficient summaries.

**Experiment:** compare false positives across one test and many searched tests.

# Week 55: Conditional expectation

[[Road to Quant/START HERE|Dashboard]] · [[Road to Quant/Projects/P05|sequential-learning-research]]

**Window:** 2027-10-20–2027-10-26. **Budget:** 20 hours; weekends are free.

**Study:** conditional expectation, sigma-algebras, tower property, and orthogonal prediction.

**Derive / solve:** derive conditional expectation in a finite partition and verify the tower property.
